en: The *Śivastuti* composed by Śrī Laṅkeśvara:

We bow to that indescribable splendor who bears blackness upon his throat, who displays the moon upon the surface of his forehead, whose mass of matted locks is gracefully sported, and whose lotus-like hands are beautiful;
who holds up a skull at his waist and displays an elephant hide upon his hips—we bow to him at every moment. (LSiv_1)
I worship Him, whose white radiance flashes upon the bull, dispelling the pride born from the majestic whiteness of Mount Kailāsa;
who is colored by the beautiful saffron from the breasts of Umā; who is resplendent with an elephant hide; and who is the seed for the destruction of all suffering.

I praise Mṛḍa, whose crest is shimmering with the waves of the celestial river as it sports in the forest of his matted locks that are ever-unfurled; and who, by day and night, through the mingling of the light radiating from his three rising eyes and the moon—the mine of digits—causes the river of immortality to surge ever more intensely.
Abandoning the dalliances of the lotus-dwelling goddess, which are so skilled at mimicking the dancing lightning,

let my mind find its wandering in the Lord Brahmā— the wearer of matted hair, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon that delights the night-lotuses, and upon whose hips the elephant-hide serves as a garment.
Indra and the other gods remain with the tips of their crowns shattered by the blows of your formidable staff-like snout against the thresholds of your celestial abodes;
O Lord of the Pramathas, why do we not abandon our divine prosperity, return to our natural state as Piśācas, and come into your presence? O Protector! We pray for this.
We hope for some mountain whose flowering and fruit-bearing trees have been plundered by the Pramatha maidens intent on worshipping you;
we have no need for Meru, where the flowers scattered by the wives of the Siddhas reclining on the terraces of its slopes are as common as dūrvā grass.
O Hara, may my mind never again indulge in the wicked play of sense-objects, nor let the tales of the Mind-born God (Kāma) ever become guests of my heart.
O Śiva, O Bhavānī, may I dwell forever at the edge of a hut on the banks of the shimmering river of erotic passion, intent upon your worship day and night.
May this Goddess—who is nurtured by the abundant spray scattered from the rows of shimmering, pure basins that serve as her celestial river of ornaments;
who is the blossoming cluster of matted locks upon the divine tree of Maheśvara; and who bestows the fruit of liberation upon those who bow before her—truly grant me [my desires], alas! 8.

I worship the digit of the moon being contemplated by the young ascetic Śiva— the soul of all beings, whose senses have been withdrawn from contact with external objects through the power of meditative absorption, and who bears upon his head the celestial river that winds like a wish-fulfilling tree.
O Lord, whose splendor resembles the pure jasmine flower, may this mind of mine enter the thicket of matted locks drenched by the streams of pure water from Your divine river,
and attain the likeness of the assembly of ascetics shining in the forest of trees on the banks of that most excellent river.
Thus ends the Śivastuti composed by Śrī Laṅkeśvara.
